Inspiration upgrades (2026-10-20, inspiration-portfolio-review.md): outcome meter, Ask Noor / Ask Dr. Omar hints, outcome-first feedback, a day-at-the-clinic spine (02), revisit map on results, replies from the other side (04, 06).

01.hook: Can you keep your clinic safe in your first week?

hs1-205.text: Think about who could get hurt in the next minute, and which fix removes the hazard rather than just warning about it. You may always stop unsafe work.

hs1-409.text: Remember the order in RACE: people first, then the alarm, then containing the fire. An alarm call needs three things: the code, where you are, and who you are.

hs1-507.text: Use one rule for every spill: how much, and how dangerous. Volume is not the only trigger. ⚠ Draft — pending D1.

hs1-802.text: An overdue inspection means nobody can vouch for this device today. Who owns medical equipment checks here?

02.hook: Can you handle a day in the safety lab?

hs2-052.text: Two questions for each spill: is it biological or chemical, and does it cross the Code Orange rule? A tiny amount can still be serious.

02.shift_title: A day in the safety lab
shift_notes: Your first walk-round: find what could hurt someone.
Smoke in a consultation room: run the Code Red drill.
Get everyone out safely, including people who can't use the stairs.
Pick and use the right extinguisher, or decide not to.
Spills in the lab and the store: triage each one.
Before handover: read the labels and the chemical register.

03.hook: Can you find your way through your first 90 days?

hr-031.text: Ask yourself: would I be comfortable if everyone could see this decision? When in doubt, declare it and ask.

hr-044.text: Check each request against the rule for that leave type: who qualifies, how long they have served, and what documents they need.

04.hook: Can you get every patient to the right team, first time?

ops-031.text: Two questions decide the route: is the patient in the clinic now, or is this about their care over the coming weeks?

n1.a: Patient: “Thank you — someone is finally looking into it.”
n1.b: Patient: “The coordinator? I'm standing right here, upset, now.”
n1.c: Patient: “So I have to come back and explain it all again?”

n2.b: Patient: “The front desk won't remember me in three months.”
n2.c: Patient: “I thought the clinic would remind me.”

n3.a: Patient: “So someone will follow up with the insurer for me?”
n3.b: Patient: “The manager doesn't deal with my insurance, surely?”
n3.c: Patient: “The pharmacy told me to ask someone else.”

n4.a: Doctor: “Thanks — the afternoon queue is hurting my clinic times.”
n4.b: Doctor: “This isn't about call quality, it's the queue.”
n4.c: Doctor: “I'm seeing patients — I can't run the pharmacy too.”

05.hook: Can you write a note that gets the claim paid?

rcma-031.text: Order what the findings and history justify, not everything you can think of. What does the note need to show to support it?

06.hook: Can you turn a rejected claim into a paid one?

rcmb-052.text: A rejection comment is a to-do list. Start where the problem began: the documentation behind the claim.

n1.a: Payer system: “Rejected again — same reason as before.”

n2.a: Payer reviewer: “Diagnosis now matches the findings.”
n2.b: Payer reviewer: “The second code isn't supported by the note — flagged.”
n2.c: Payer reviewer: “Still a symptom code — same rejection.”

n3.a: Payer system: “Resubmission received with supporting document — under review.”
n3.b: Payer system: “Duplicate claim for the same visit — rejected.”

07.hook: Can you stop harm before it reaches a patient?

qsr-021.text: A name alone is never enough. What does policy say you check, and what is never an identifier?

qsr-051.text: No harm doesn't mean nothing to report. Near misses are how we learn before anyone is hurt. ⚠ Draft — pending D8.

08.hook: Can you close a consultation without a single gap?
